output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes lean clearly hawkish. On inflation, participants judged they "had not seen sufficient progress on lowering inflation," with several citing elevated core services ex-housing and core goods, some saying underlying inflation was above 2 percent and moving sideways, and several noting elevated short-term inflation expectations; only a few pointed to a disinflationary 3-month measure and some saw wage growth as benign. On the labor market, a majority saw recent strengthening and participants generally viewed labor-market risks as balanced. On risks, inflation risks were generally seen as skewed to the upside (more so recently per some), with many citing elevated energy prices and several citing possible tariff increases. On policy, most participants assessed another increase would likely be appropriate by year end, many favored a higher path on risk-management grounds, a number saw it as necessary on their modal outlooks, and several viewed the rate as not or only mildly restrictive. What would change their minds: incoming information and the balance of risks, approached with an open mind each meeting. With the next decision on 2026-10-28, these minutes imply a hawkish tilt (+7 bp).

On inflation, participants said it "remained elevated" with insufficient recent progress; several cited elevated core services ex-housing and core goods inflation, some judged underlying inflation above 2% and moving sideways, and several noted elevated short-term inflation expectations. On risks, participants generally assessed inflation risk skewed to the upside—many tied to elevated energy prices, several to possible tariff increases, and some to expectations un-anchoring. On policy, all participants backed the 25 bp hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent; many framed a higher path as prudent insurance, a number saw it as necessary on their modal outlooks, several saw policy as not or only mildly restrictive, and crucially "most participants assessed that another increase ... would likely be appropriate by year end." What would change minds: they approached each meeting "with an open mind" and future decisions "would depend on incoming information and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks." Net lean: hawkish.

On inflation, participants judged it "remained elevated" with insufficient recent progress; "several" saw elevated core services and core goods prices, "some" said underlying inflation is above 2% and moving sideways, and "several" noted elevated short-term inflation expectations. Dovish notes were limited: "a few" cited a declining 3-month core PCE measure (but cautioned it is volatile) and "some" said wage growth was moderate and not a source of inflation pressure, while "several" flagged unusually low labor market dynamism. On the labor market, participants viewed it near maximum employment, "a majority" assessed it had "strengthened a bit recently," and risks were "broadly balanced." Inflation risks were generally "skewed to the upside," with "many," "several," and "some" citing energy, tariffs, AI demand, and expectations-anchoring concerns. On policy, all supported the 25bp hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent; "almost all" saw inflation risks tilted up with labor risks diminished; "many" favored a higher path on risk-management grounds, "a number" on their modal outlooks, "several" saw policy as not or only mildly restrictive, and crucially "most" assessed another increase would likely be appropriate by year end. What would change minds: future decisions "would depend on incoming information and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks." Given "most" expecting a further year-end hike and broad upside inflation risk, the net lean toward the Oct 28 decision is hawkish.

output.summary: The minutes lean clearly hawkish. Participants said inflation "remained elevated" with insufficient progress; several saw elevated core services ex-housing and core goods inflation, some judged underlying inflation above 2 percent and moving sideways, and several flagged elevated short-term inflation expectations. On risks, participants generally assessed inflation risk "skewed to the upside," with some seeing it more skewed recently, and cited energy prices, the AI buildout, and possible further tariffs as upside risks. On the labour market, a majority judged it had "strengthened a bit recently" and almost all said labour-market risks had "diminished and were now broadly balanced," though several noted unusually low dynamism and some said wages were not a source of inflation (dovish offsets). On policy, all supported the September hike, many favoured a higher path on risk-management grounds, a number saw it necessary on modal outlooks, several saw the rate as not or only mildly restrictive, and "most participants" expected another increase would likely be appropriate by year end. The main dovish caveats are balanced labour-market risks, low labour dynamism, moderate wage comments, and the open-mind, data-dependent language. On net, with the next decision on 2026-10-28 and most expecting a further hike by year end, the implied tilt is hawkish (+6 bp).

output.summary: The September 15–16, 2026 minutes are decisively hawkish for the October 28 decision. Participants judged inflation still elevated with insufficient progress, assessed inflation risks as skewed to the upside, and viewed the labor market as near maximum employment with some signs of strengthening. All participants backed the 25bp hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, several saw policy as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive, and "most participants" expected another increase would likely be appropriate by year end — a window that includes the next meeting. The main offsetting notes are that labor-market risks were seen as broadly balanced and that decisions remain data-dependent ("open mind"). Net lean: hawkish.
